chapter_theme: Poems 1-20 open with the invocation to the god of the konrai and then praise and counsel the three crowned lines: counsel (செவியறிவுறூஉ) on giving, impartiality and guarding the realm like a child, vanji poems that boast of burned enemy fields, questions about gifts paid for by conquest, and Kudapulaviyanar's argument that the king who stores water gives life.

1.reading: An invocation that names the god only by his marks: a wreath and garland of konrai, the white bull as mount and banner, the dark stain on the throat that Vedic brahmins speak of, a woman's form that is one part of him and that he may also hide within himself, the crescent on his brow praised by the eighteen hosts, and the ever-full water pot and hanging matted locks of the great ascetic who is a refuge to all living beings.
1.nuance: Each mark is stated and then given a second clause that raises it (the stain is also spoken of by the brahmins; the crescent is also praised by the hosts), so the poem is built in pairs. The woman-form clause goes further than the usual half-woman image: the god can also conceal her within himself (கரக்கினும் கரக்கும்). The name Siva is never used.

thinai_evidence.note: praise of a god by his marks, the கடவுள் வாழ்த்து that porul 2.27 sets under paadaan

2.reading: Murinjiyur Mudinagarayar praises the Chera Uthiyan Cheralathan, whose forbearance, breadth of counsel, strength, fierceness and grace match the nature of the five elements, in whose sea the sun rises and in whose western sea it sets, who gave food without limit while the hundred fought the five until they fell; he wishes him to stand unshaken with his unwavering kin, even if milk turns sour, day turns dark and the Vedas' way changes, like the Himalaya and Pothiyam where deer sleep by the light of the brahmins' evening fires.
2.nuance: Lines 13 to 16 tie the patron's name (பெருஞ்சோறு, great food) to the war of the five and the hundred, the earliest Tamil reference to that war; the poem says only that he gave food without limit until the hundred fell, not to whom. The blessing works by impossibilities (milk souring, day darkening, the Veda's path changing), so the king's steadiness is set beyond the order of nature itself.

thinai_evidence.note: praise of the king's giving with a blessing that he endure

comparisons.tenor: the king's forbearance, counsel, strength, fierceness and grace
the king standing unshaken with his kin

3.reading: Irumpidarthalaiyar praises the Pandya Vazhuthi of the black hand and bright sword, scion of the Kauriyar, whose white umbrella like the full moon shades the sea-girt earth and whose word does not move even if the earth moves, and counsels him that suppliants come longing for him across waterless, townless roads where bowmen in ambush shoot travellers and kites sit grieving on their fresh stone-heaps, so that his true strength is to read their need from their faces and end their poverty.
3.nuance: The counsel is compressed into the last two and a half lines, and its weight falls on line 25: the giver should know the need from the face before it is spoken. The road passage (lines 17 to 23) does work for the counsel: it is the price the suppliants have already paid to come. The kites on the fresh cairns are a scene, not an image of the king.

thinai_evidence.note: praise of the king closing in counsel on giving to suppliants

comparisons.tenor: the king's tall white umbrella

4.reading: Paranar describes the Chola's war gear after battle, each in a simile (swords red like the evening sky, feet like the horns of a killing bull, shields pierced like a fixed target, horses red-mouthed like a tiger that has seized a neck, elephants with blunted tusks like Death that eats lives), sets the king on his golden chariot like the red sun rising from the sea, and ends that the lands of those who angered him cry without ceasing like a child its mother has not fed.
4.nuance: The poem is a chain of seven comparisons, five of them in the same frame (thing, its battle mark, போன்றன), so the king is approached through his gear before he is named as the sun. Only the last simile turns from the victor to the victim: the enemy country as an unfed infant, which is the lament that gives the thurai its name.

thinai_evidence.note: the king's battle and the wailing of the enemy's land after his invasion

comparisons.tenor: the swords stained in victory
the king's legs, their anklets worn in battle
the shields pierced again and again by arrows
the horses with mouths reddened by the bit
the elephants that battered the gates
the king on his golden chariot
the enemy lands crying ceaselessly

5.reading: Nariveruuthalaiyar tells the Chera, lord of a forest land where elephants spread like cattle among black rocks like buffaloes, that since he is such a man he will say one thing: do not side with those who cast off grace and love and take a hell that never leaves; guard the realm as those who rear a child, for that guarding is a thing of grace and hard to come by.
5.nuance: The opening picture is double: rocks like buffaloes and elephants like cattle make the wild forest a pasture, which prepares the counsel that the king should be a herdsman and nurse. The comparisons in lines 2 and 7 use the comparative -இன் (ஆனிற், பவரின்) rather than அன்ன or போல. What அது in line 8 refers to (the guarding, the realm, or the reward of guarding) is not fixed by the syntax.

thinai_evidence.note: counsel spoken to the king, the செவியறிவுறூஉ of paadaan

comparisons.tenor: the black rocks
the elephants spreading among the rocks
the king guarding his realm

6.reading: Karikizhar wishes the Pandya Mudukudumi, whose form and fame reach from beyond the Himalaya to below Kumari, from sea to sea and from the waters below to the world above, that he may lean to no side like the beam of a balance, that his umbrella bow only in circling the three-eyed god's shrine, his head only before the raised hands of the Vedic sages, his garland wilt only in the smoke of burned enemy lands and his anger yield only to his women's sulking faces, and that he abide on earth like the cool moon and the burning sun.
6.nuance: Four optative clauses (பணியியர், இறைஞ்சுக, வாடுக, செலிஇயர்) map where the king should give way and where he should not; the paired moon and sun at the close repeat the split between mildness and heat. The giving of captured jewels to bards in due order (வரிசையின்) is placed inside the praise of conquest, so the plunder is legitimated by its distribution.

thinai_evidence.note: blessing and counsel to a king

comparisons.tenor: the king, who should hold to no one side
the king abiding on earth, cool to his own
the king abiding on earth, burning to his foes

7.reading: Karunkuzhal Athanar praises Karikalan, whose feet drive elephants, whose hand is bent from the bow and whose chest has turned back horses, for taking no account of day or night and delighting in plunder amid the wailing in the light of burning enemy towns, so that the good things are no more in others' wide, rich lands where cool floods spread and are held back by fish.
7.nuance: The praise has a sting: நல்ல இல்ல ஆகுபவால் (the good things come to be gone) is said to the king, and the last three lines spend their richest description on the lands he ruins. The exact sense of lines 11 and 12 (a flood held back not by earth but by fish) is a hyperbole of plenty whose syntax is not certain.

thinai_evidence.note: the king's raid, burning towns and taking plunder

8.reading: Kapilar asks the sun how it could equal Cheralathan, whom the world's kings obey, who will not bear the earth being called common to others and finds it too small, of unshrinking heart and unsparing gifts: the sun keeps set hours, turns its back and goes, comes back changed, hides behind the hills, and shines only by day.
8.nuance: The comparison is denied: each of the sun's motions (keeping hours, turning away, changing, hiding, shining only by day) becomes a lack set against the king's constancy. ஊக்கம் is named in line 3 as the drive that finds the earth too small (இடம் சிறிது), a praise that also admits his ambition.

thinai_evidence.note: praise of the king by refusing him a comparison

comparisons.tenor: Cheralathan, whom the sun cannot match

9.reading: Nettimaiyar blesses the Pandya Kudumi, who before battle proclaims the way of dharma, telling cows, brahmin-natured men, women, the sick and those without sons to perform the rites for the ancestors to go to shelter before he lets fly his arrows, and wishes him years more than the sands of the Pahruli river of the ancient Pandya Nediyon, who gave fresh gold to dancers at the sea festival.
9.nuance: The opening quotation is the king's own war proclamation, and its list defines who is outside war: animals of the household, priests, women, the sick, and men whose line would end with them. The blessing reaches back to Nediyon and the Pahruli, linking this Pandya to a legendary ancestor's generosity.

thinai_evidence.note: praise and blessing of the king's righteous conduct of war

comparisons.tenor: sons who can perform the rites for the ancestors
the years the poet wishes the king

10.reading: Oonpothi Pasunkudaiyar praises the Chola of Neythalankanal, who knows well those who serve him, does not believe those who slander others, punishes a proven wrong after weighing it fairly and lessens the penalty when the offender comes and stands at his feet, whose house feeds all comers, and whose chest only women now fight with since warriors have given up fighting him; the poet has come to him to praise him at length.
10.nuance: The chest that only women 'fight' (மலைத்தல், also to wear or embrace) while warriors have stopped fighting it is a pun that sets love-quarrel against war. Mercy here follows submission, not rank: the softened penalty is for the one who comes and holds the king's feet.

thinai_evidence.note: praise of the king's justice and hospitality by a poet come to him

11.reading: Peymagal Ilaveyiniyar tells how, by the cool Porunai where girls with fine jewels pick flowers for their sand dolls and plunge into the water, the Chera king worthy of the vanji song crossed a fierce fortress and saw his enemies' backs; the singer who sang that valour received fine gold jewels, and her partner the bard, skilled in tune, received a gold lotus strung on silver thread.
11.nuance: The poem never asks; it lists who received what (the king, the enemy's backs; the singer, jewels; the bard, the lotus), and the request is left for the next link, the poet herself, which is how பரிசில் கடாநிலை works here. விறல்வஞ்சிப் பாடல் is the vanji song of victory, not the Chera town Vanji.

thinai_evidence.note: a chain of gifts received from the king, which asks for a gift by telling of others'

12.reading: Nettimaiyar asks the Pandya Kudumi whether it is dharma that bards wear gold lotuses and poets are given chariots with elephants, when he takes others' land so that it is painful to them and does what is sweet before those who love him.
12.nuance: The five lines can be read as playful praise (so generous it is almost wrong) or as a real question about gifts paid for by conquest; the poem gives no answer, and the pairing இன்னா ... இனிய holds the two sides of the same act together.

thinai_evidence.note: address to a king about his gifts

13.reading: Mudamosiyar answers someone who asks who the man is: the one on the Death-like elephant, his armour torn by arrows, while the elephant, like a ship on the sea and the moon among many stars, surrounded by swordsmen like a shoal of sharks, has gone wild beyond its keepers' control; may he return unharmed, the lord of a land of water-fenced fields where ploughmen gather dropped peacock feathers with their sheaves and fish and toddy abound.
13.nuance: The poem turns from danger to plenty without transition: the last four lines describe the king's home country so richly that the wish for his return becomes a picture of what he must return to. Who asks 'who is he?' and where the elephant has run are not stated in the poem.

thinai_evidence.note: a blessing for a king's safe return

comparisons.tenor: the elephant the king rides
the elephant moving through the army
the king on his elephant among his soldiers
the swordsmen thronging round

14.reading: Kapilar tells the Chera that his knee-long hands are hard, since they drive the elephant to break the crossbars, rein the horses at the deep moat, are scarred by the bowstring and give rare jewels to suppliants, while the hands of the poets who sing him are very soft, since they know no work but eating meat smoked with fragrant smoke, mashed meat and rice with curry.
14.nuance: The contrast is playful self-mockery: the king's hands are praised through the softness of the poets' own, which is the proof of his feeding. The hard hands do four labours, and the last of them is giving, so generosity is counted among the toils of war.

thinai_evidence.note: praise of the king's deeds and gifts through the poets' own hands

comparisons.tenor: the king's firmness toward his foes
the king as Murugan in battle

15.reading: Nettimaiyar asks the Pandya Kudumi which are more: the enemies who came wanting to take the head of his vanguard and went away living in shame, or the wide fields where he planted sacrificial posts after completing Vedic sacrifices with ghee offerings, after he had ploughed their walled towns with white-mouthed donkeys, driven his chariots over their bird-loud fields and bathed his elephants in their guarded tanks.
15.nuance: The closing question (யாபல கொல்லோ) leaves war and sacrifice uncounted and equal, so the Vedic rite and the razing of cities are praised in one breath. Ploughing a conquered town with donkeys is a rite of ruin, the opposite of the ploughing that founds a field.

thinai_evidence.note: praise of the king that sets his wars against his sacrifices

16.reading: Pandarangannanar tells the Chola Perunarkilli that his army, with swift horses and shields spread like clouds, broke the enemy front, fed on their ripe fields, burned their house-beams as firewood, bathed elephants at their guarded ghats and lit fires glowing like the setting sun, so that the great cool fields that knew no wood but sugarcane, with vallai, ambal, pakanrai and pagal, became waste, and his elephants fought as one.
16.nuance: The fields are described at their richest (a land whose only 'forest' is sugarcane) in the same breath as they are made waste, so the beauty of the enemy's land is the measure of the king's might. The water plants are listed as what was there before the burning.

thinai_evidence.note: the invasion and burning of an enemy's farmland

comparisons.tenor: the shields spread out
the glow of the burning fires
the king's anger

17.reading: Kurunkozhiyur Kizhar praises the Chera Irumporai, heir of kings who ruled the whole land from Kumari to the northern mountain and from sea to sea with a straight sceptre, lord of cool Thondi of screwpine, fields, sandy groves and backwaters, who escaped his great distress as a tusker fallen into a covered pit breaks its bank and rejoins its rejoicing herd, so that enemy kings, fearing to lose their walls and moats, began to submit; the poet has come to see the king of the Kudavar, with shields like clouds, elephants like hills, an army like the sea and a drum like thunder.
17.nuance: The pit simile (lines 14 to 21) implies a captivity or reverse from which the king broke free, but the poem names neither; the enemy kings' two quoted thoughts (we might regain our land if he is pleased; we shall lose our walls, he looked at us in anger) are a rare piece of the defeated's reasoning.

thinai_evidence.note: praise of a king's might and the submission of rival kings

comparisons.tenor: the king escaping his distress to his kin's joy
the many shields
the great elephants on which bees build
the army swelling to fight
the roar of the drum

18.reading: Kudapulaviyanar blesses the Pandya Nedunchezhiyan, lord of an old city with a moat full of fish and a wall the sky fears, and tells him that whether he wants wealth in the next world, sole rule over the kings of this one, or lasting fame, he should hear what is fitting: bodies cannot live without water, food makes the body, food is land joined with water, so those who join land and water give body and life; land that sows and waits on the sky does not help its ruler however wide, so he should quickly build up tanks where the land dips, for those who bind water here have bound those goals, and those who do not have not.
18.nuance: The argument is a chain (water, food, body, life) closed by a pun on தட்டோர்: those who dammed (water) are those who secured (the three goals), and those who did not, did not. All three royal ambitions of lines 13 to 16, including heaven, are made to depend on irrigation.

colophon.thurai: முதுமொழிக் காஞ்சி : பொருண்மொழிக் காஞ்சி எனவும் பாடம்

thinai_evidence.note: counsel of general truth to a king, the காஞ்சி that the later scheme files under pothuviyal

19.reading: Kudapulaviyanar recalls, before the Pandya who defeated the seven at Thalaiyalanganam, where Tamils clashed and he alone was weighed against Death, that he embraced the king's chest thinking it like a stone deadfall set by a tiger-hunter, and describes the dreadful field where elephants with severed trunks rolled like ploughs and the women of old houses wept, 'our little sons lie with our fathers: is such valour ours?', so that Death fled ashamed; he asks if this is the chest wearing the bright garland.
19.nuance: Line 3 weighs the king against Death (the many lives against Death's singleness), and line 16 has Death flee ashamed, so the battle is told as a contest the king won against Death itself. The mothers' cry, 'is there such valour for us?', joins grief and pride in one sentence, and the poem lets them stand together.

thinai_evidence.note: praise of the king's victory in a named battle

comparisons.vehicle: இரும்புலி வேட்டுவன் பொறிஅறிந்து மாட்டிய பெருங்கல் அடாரும்
comparisons.tenor: the king's chest
the arrows lodged in the elephant
the severed elephant trunks rolling on the ground

20.reading: Kurunkozhiyur Kizhar tells the Chera that though one might measure the sea's depth, the earth's breadth, the wind's ways and the empty sky, his knowledge, compassion and kindness are beyond measure; those in his shade know no burning but the cooking fire and the sun, no bow but the rainbow, no weapon but the plough; enemies never eat his land's soil, which only craving pregnant women eat; his fortress lets arrows sleep and his sceptre lets dharma rest; his guard is not shaken by omen birds coming or going; so all living beings fear for him.
20.nuance: The poem works by exclusions (no burning but..., no bow but the rainbow, திருவில் against கொலைவில்), so the realm's peace is described through what its people do not know. The last line, மன்னுயிர் எல்லாம் நின் அஞ்சும், can mean all beings fear you or fear for you; the praise of a peaceful realm favours the second.

thinai_evidence.note: praise of a king's qualities and the peace of his realm rather than a victory

links.note: Both name the god by his marks, the konrai, the matted hair and the woman who is part of him; Purananuru 1 lists them without a name, Tirumanthiram 16 calls him the one whose part is the bright-browed woman.
links.teaches: Set beside Tirumular, the anthology's invocation shows that konrai, matted hair and the woman-part were already a fixed set of marks that identified the god without his name, and it adds what Tirumular's verse lacks: the god may also hide that female form within himself.

links.note: 3 ends by calling the ending of suppliants' poverty the king's true strength (வன்மை); Kural 225 ranks the strength of removing others' hunger above the strength of enduring one's own.
links.teaches: The Kural's ranking of strengths is abstract, and the Pandya counsel turns it into a test of practice: the giver must read the need from the face before it is spoken, and the deadly road the suppliants crossed measures what that strength owes them.

links.note: 5 tells the king not to side with those who cast off grace (அருள்) and love and take a hell that never leaves; Kural 243 says those whose hearts hold அருள் do not enter the dark, painful world.
links.teaches: The Kural makes grace a person's safeguard against hell; the Chera counsel turns the same link into a rule of government, where grace is shown by guarding the realm as one rears a child and hell is the lot of rulers who drop it.

links.note: Both use the weighing balance for leaning to no side: 6 wishes the king may not hold to one side, like the beam of a balance (தெரிகோல் ஞமன்ன் போல); Kural 118 makes not leaning, like a levelled scale, the ornament of the worthy.
links.teaches: The same balance serves as a king's blessing in the Purananuru and as a general virtue in the Kural, which shows that impartiality was pictured as a public act of weighing done by whoever judges, before it was a disposition of the private person.

links.note: Kural 978 says greatness always bows; 6 asks the king's umbrella and head to bow before the god's shrine and the sages, his garland to wilt only in the smoke of burned enemy lands, and his anger to yield before his women's sulking.
links.teaches: Where the Kural makes humility a constant trait of the great, the Purananuru poet gives it addresses: the king bows to god, sages and wives and to no one on the field, so royal humility was a question of before whom, not of always.

links.note: 9 praises the Pandya who, before battle, tells cows, brahmins, women, the sick and the sonless to take shelter; Kural 773 calls generous help to the foe in misfortune the cutting edge of valour.
links.teaches: The Kural puts mercy at the end of valour, once the foe has fallen; the Purananuru shows a king putting it before the first arrow by warning those who cannot fight, so the restraint of the brave had a set procedure as well as a maxim.

links.note: 10 says the Chola, seeing a proven wrong, weighs it fairly and punishes fittingly (ஒப்ப நாடி அத்தக ஒறுத்தி); Kural 561 defines a king as one who inquires fittingly and punishes in proportion (தக்காங்கு நாடி ... ஒத்தாங்கு ஒறுப்பது).
links.teaches: The two share the very words for inquiry and proportion, so the Kural's definition of the just king reads like a rule drawn out of praise such as this, and 10 adds what 561 leaves out: the sentence is softened for the one who comes and stands at the king's feet.

links.note: Kural 541 makes justice an inquiry without favour to anyone (கண்ணோடாது); 10 praises a king who lessens the penalty when the offender submits.
links.teaches: Read together they show that the old ideal allowed mercy after the verdict but not favour within it: the Kural bars kindly regard in the inquiry, while the Purananuru king reduces the sentence for submission, not for kinship or closeness.

links.note: 11 lists as glory the gold jewels and the silver-strung gold lotus a conquering Chera gave his singer and bard; 12 asks a Pandya whether giving bards gold lotuses and poets chariots is dharma when it comes from land taken to others' pain.
links.teaches: Side by side, the two poems show that the anthology did not take the gift economy on trust: the gold lotus that crowns the bard in 11 becomes in 12 a question about where a king's gifts come from.

links.note: 12 asks whether gifts made from others' land, taken so that it pains them, are dharma; Kural 659 says all that is taken with tears leaves with tears.
links.teaches: Nettimaiyar leaves his question to the king, and the Kural answers it with a law of return, which shows that the poet's courteous irony carries a real moral charge against the plunder that pays for the bards' gifts.

links.note: 14 praises the king's hands, hardened by goad, bowstring and giving, against the soft hands of his poets, which do nothing but eat; Kural 1035 honours those who eat from their own hands' work, who do not beg and who give to those who ask.
links.teaches: In the Kural the hand that works for its food is the hand that gives; Kapilar reverses the order and makes the poets' soft, idle hands the proof of the patron's care, so the court valued being fed as a sign of the giver's greatness where the Kural values self-support.

links.note: Both praise the same Pandya, Mudukudumi: 9 for warning cows, brahmins, women and the sick to shelter before battle; 15 for ploughing enemy towns with donkeys, driving chariots over their fields and bathing his elephants in their guarded tanks.
links.teaches: The pair shows that the righteous warning of 9 limited whom the king would kill, not what he would destroy: the same king who spares cows and the sick ploughs the enemy city into waste.

links.note: 16 praises a Chola for turning cool sugarcane fields into waste and feeding fire to a safe land; 18 tells a Pandya that food is land joined with water and that those who give food give life.
links.teaches: The anthology holds both the vanji boast of burned farmland and the counsel that farmland is life, which shows that the counsel of 18 was a duty owed to one's own land, while the enemy's fields remained a fit measure of glory.

links.note: 17 praises the Irumporai as lord of cool Thondi, with screwpine, wide fields, sandy groves and backwaters; Akananuru 60 compares a fisherman's guarded daughter's beauty to Thondi of the Porayan of the strong chariots.
links.teaches: The Poraiyan port that the praise poet counts among the king's possessions became, in akam, the standard for a girl's well-guarded beauty, which shows love poets taking their measure of value from the Chera wealth that puram poets praised.

links.note: Kural 542 says the whole world lives looking to the sky and the people to the ruler's sceptre; 18 says land that sows and looks to the sky (வித்திவான் நோக்கும் புன்புலம்) does not help its ruler however wide, and tells him to build tanks.
links.teaches: Where the Kural sets rain and the sceptre side by side as the two things people depend on, Kudapulaviyanar makes the ruler answerable for freeing the land from the sky, turning dependence on rain into a duty of public works.

links.note: 18 opens its argument with bodies that cannot exist without water (நீர்இன்று அமையா யாக்கை); Kural 20 says the world cannot go on without water (நீர்இன்று அமையாது உலகு).
links.teaches: The two share the phrase but draw different conclusions from it: the Kural derives the world's dependence on the sky, the Purananuru the king's duty to store water, so one premise supported both a praise of rain and a policy against relying on it.

links.note: Both name Nedunchezhiyan's victory over the seven at Alankanam (ஆலங் கானத்து; எழுவர் நல்வலம்): 19 shows the field where mothers wept and Death fled ashamed, Akananuru 36 makes the victors' shout there the measure of how loud the gossip about the hero is.
links.teaches: The akam poet borrowed only the victors' roar from Alankanam to measure a scandal, while the puram poem on the same battle keeps the weeping of the old houses' women, so one battle served love poetry as a byword for noise and praise poetry as a field of grief.

links.note: 20 ends: all living beings fear (அஞ்சும்) you; Kural 563 says a ruler who acts so as to cause dread perishes quickly. On the reading that the beings fear the king, 20 praises what the Kural condemns; on the reading that they fear for him, the two agree.
links.teaches: The ambiguity of 20's last line matters because the Kural's chapter against causing dread makes a feared king a doomed king, so Kurunkozhiyur Kizhar's praise only holds if the people's fear is anxiety for their ruler and not dread of him.

new_concepts.gloss: the gift a bard seeks from a patron, and the asking for it
new_concepts.label_source: the colophons use the word: பரிசில் கடாநிலை for poem 11; பரிசிலர் in 14 line 10

source_issues: 1: the colophon has no thinai or thurai (both null); the poem is the anthology's invocation (கடவுள் வாழ்த்து), marked here as paadaan. The patron field reads இறைவன், a description, not a name.
2 line 23: விளக்கிற், றுஞ்சும் puts a comma inside a sandhi join (விளக்கின் + துஞ்சும் gives விளக்கிற் றுஞ்சும்); the comma belongs after துஞ்சும் or nowhere.
